reading: See how the excellent painter has made the Trojan boy
carried through the highest stars by the bird of Jupiter.
Would anyone believe that Jupiter was touched by love for a boy?
Tell me, where did the Maeonian old man [Homer] invent this?
Counsel, mind, and joy in God — the one to whom these are given
is believed to be snatched up and to stand before highest Jupiter.

greek.translation: “To rejoice in counsels”, Ganymede [the name is explained from the Greek words].

2.motto: Human wisdom is folly before God.

reading: What shall I say? By what name shall I call this monster,
two-formed, which is neither man nor dragon?
Rather, a man without feet, a snake without upper parts —
it can be called a snake-footed man and a man-headed snake.
The man passes out a snake [from below], and the snake has belched out a man,
and the man has no end, the beast no beginning.
So once Cecrops reigned in learned Athens,
so too mother earth brought forth the giants.
This is an image of the crafty; but it points to one who lacks religion
and cares only for earthly things.
Seated on a royal throne, a most beautiful harlot
wears a robe distinguished by the honour of purple,
and to all she offers drink from a full mixing bowl,
while around her a drunken crowd lies sprawling.
So they represent Babylon, which with an enticing appearance
and feigned religion captures foolish nations.

4.motto: Not to you, but to religion.

reading: A slow little ass was carrying the image of Isis,
bearing the revered mysteries on its bent back.
So everyone who meets it reverently worships the goddess
and offers pious prayers on bended knees.
But the ass believes that such honour is shown
to itself, and swells up, very proud,
until the driver, checking it with the whip, said:
“You are not a god, little ass, but you carry a god.”

5.motto: One must go where the gods call.

reading: At a crossroads there is a heap of stones; above it rises
a truncated image of the god, made down to the breast.
This, then, is the mound of Mercury. Hang up, traveller,
garlands to the god: he shows you the right road.
We are all at a crossroads, and on this path of life
we go astray unless God himself shows the way.
Let Honor stand depicted, clothed in a Tyrian cloak,
and let naked Truth join her right hand with his.
And in the middle let there be chaste Love: around his temples
goes a rose; he is fairer than Dione's Cupid.
These signs make up faith: reverence for Honor
cherishes it, Love nourishes it, and Truth gives birth to it.
This lute, which from the shape of a boat is called the “fisherman's”,
and which the Latin Muse claims as her own,
accept, Duke: may our gift please you at this time,
when you are preparing to enter new alliances with your allies.
It is hard, unless one is skilled, to tune so many strings;
and if a single string (fides) is not well stretched
or breaks (which is easy), all the charm of the shell [the instrument] is lost,
and that surpassing song will be out of tune.
So the Italian princes come together in alliances: when there is concord
there is nothing for you to fear, if love stands firm for you.
But if someone falls away (as we generally see),
all that harmony dissolves into nothing.
When he is silent, the fool differs in nothing from the wise.
His tongue and voice are the informers of his folly.
So let him press his lips together, mark silence with his finger,
and turn himself into Pharian Harpocrates.

9.motto: Plans are not to be divulged.

reading: The monster which Daedalus shut up behind a blind threshold and in dark gloom
in the Cnossian hiding places,
the Roman phalanx carries depicted into battle,
and the standards shine proudly with the half-man bull.
They remind us that the secret plans of leaders ought to stay hidden:
a stratagem once known harms its author.

10.motto: Not to yield even to torture.

reading: The lioness you see sculpted in the citadel of Cecrops
was the mistress of Hermodius (do you not know, stranger?).
So they chose to show the fierce spirit of a manly woman,
in the form of a beast, or because she bore such a name [Leaena, “lioness”].
Because, racked on the cords, she betrayed no one
by her testimony, Iphicrates made her tongueless.

11.motto: The Chimaera is overcome by counsel and courage, that is, the stronger and the deceivers.

reading: Bellerophon (as a brave horseman) was able to overcome the Chimaera
and lay low the monsters of the Lycian land.
So you too, borne on the wings of Pegasus, seek the upper air
and by the counsel of your mind tame proud monsters.
Because the cock, by crowing, gives signs of the approaching dawn
and calls the hands of the maidservants back to new spinning,
he is depicted on sacred towers; [and] the bronze basin [bell], because
it calls the wakeful mind back to the gods above [?].
There is also the lion; but because this guardian sleeps with open eyes,
he is therefore placed before the doors of temples.

13.motto: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν. (“Be sober and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind.”) Live soberly, and do not believe rashly.

reading: “Do not believe, and do not be unsober,” says Epicharmus:
these will be the sinews and limbs of the human mind.
Here is the eyed hand, believing what it sees. Here
is pennyroyal (pulegium), the herb of ancient sobriety,
by showing which Heraclitus calmed the crowd
and soothed it when it was heavy with swelling sedition.

greek.original: Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησ' ἀπιστεῖν. ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν.
greek.translation: Be sober and remember to distrust: these are the joints of the mind.

14.motto: Πῆ παρέβην? Τί [?] ἔρεξα? Τί μοι δέον, οὐκ ἐτελέσθη? (“Where did I transgress? What [?] did I do? What that I ought to have done was left undone?”) In what have I exceeded? What have I committed? What have I omitted?

reading: The Samian [Pythagoras], most famous founder of the Italian school,
himself enclosed his teaching in a short verse:
“Where have you gone beyond? What are you doing? What do you leave undone that should be done?” —
urging everyone to render this account to himself.
This he is said to have learned from the flock of flying cranes,
which carry a stone seized in their feet,
so as not to stop and so that evil winds do not sweep them off course.
By this rule the life of men was to be governed.

greek.original: Πῆ παρέβην? Τί [?] ἔρεξα? Τί μοι δέον, οὐκ ἐτελέσθη?
greek.translation: Where did I transgress? What [?] did I do? What that I ought to have done was left undone?

reading: Two-faced Janus, you who know both what is past and what is to come,
and who see mockeries behind you (as also in front),
why do they portray you with so many eyes, so many faces? Is it because
the form teaches that you were a circumspect man?
The owl serves as the emblem of Cecropian Athens,
the owl, among birds the bird of sound counsel.
Deservedly she is consecrated to the service of arms-bearing Minerva,
in the place which the chattering crow had formerly given up.
All bid us to make haste quickly and to delay:
not too headlong, nor with too long a delay.
Let this be shown to you by the dart joined to the remora:
the fish is slow, while darts sent from the hand fly.
For a long time I have pursued you wherever you fled; but now
at last you are here, caught in our nets.
No longer will you be able to elude our strength:
we have gripped the eel in a fig leaf.
This is the true image of unwed Pallas; and this is her
dragon, which stands at the feet of its mistress.
Why is this animal the goddess's companion? To it has been given
the guarding of things; so it keeps the groves and sacred temples.
Unwed girls must be protected with ever-wakeful
care: love sets snares everywhere.
This temple is held in common by both, father Bacchus and Pallas,
each a true offspring of Jupiter:
she released his head, he his thigh; to her the use of the olive
is owed, but he first discovered unmixed wine.
They are joined deservedly; and if any abstainer hates
wine, he will feel no help from the goddess.
Why do you trouble me, branches? I am the tree of Pallas:
take the grapes away from here. The virgin flees from Bromius.
Father Bacchus, who has known you with mortal eye,
and who has carved your limbs with skilled hand?
Praxiteles, who saw me carrying off the Cnossian maid [Ariadne],
and portrayed me as I was at that time.
Why are you young, and why does your beard still bloom
with tender down, though you could surpass [in years] the old man of Pylos [Nestor]?
If you learn sometimes to spare my gifts,
you too will always be younger and strong of breast.
Neither drums in your hands nor horns on your head are lacking.
Whom (unless madmen) do such signs befit?
This I teach: whoever has abused our gift puts on
horns, and in his madness shakes soft sistra.
What does that almost fiery colour of your limbs mean? (may the omen
be absent) are you yourself burned on human hearths?
When my father drew me with the thunderbolt from Semele's womb,
fire-spewing, he plunged me, smeared with ash, into the waters.
Hence he is wise who dilutes us well with flowing water,
who does not scorch his liver with burning fire.
But now teach me how you wish to be mixed, and by what
law a sane man may take you safely?
Let him add a quarter of water, whoever wishes to drink
a cup of Falernian: in this way cups are pleasant to take [?].
Stay within [two] heminae: for whoever strives to go
further is merry, but soon, drunk, he raves.
This is too hard a thing. Throats are eager [lit. “hanging”], and you
flow sweetly. Alas, no good things come easily.
The fathers [senators] gave Fabius a crown of grass
because by delay he had broken the Carthaginians and Hannibal.
The lark hides her nest for herself in bent grass;
so, it is commonly said, she keeps her chicks warm.
[The grass] is sacred to Saturn and Mars; by eating it Glaucus,
son of Polybus, is believed to have become a god.
By these knots [of grass] protection and safety are rightly signified;
and this finger-grass is green, which has so many [properties] [?].

24.motto: One must harm no one by word or deed.

reading: Nemesis follows and keeps watch on the footsteps of men,
and holds in her hand a cubit [measuring rod] and a hard bridle,
so that you do nothing wrongly and speak no wicked words,
and she bids that measure be present in all things.

25.motto: At last, at last justice prevails.

reading: The shield of Aeacus' descendant [Achilles], drenched with Hector's blood,
which the unjust assembly of the Greeks gave to the Ithacan [Ulysses],
the more just Neptune seized when it was cast into the sea
in the shipwreck, so that it might reach its own master.
For the wave carried it to the shore-side mound of Ajax;
it roars and beats on the tomb with such a voice:
“You have won, son of Telamon, you are more worthy of the arms.”
It is right for partiality to yield to justice.
After the bitter plague of his country,
by killing Cicero, had destroyed Roman eloquence,
he mounted a chariot as victor and yoked lions,
and forced their necks to bear the hard yoke:
Antony wished to show that the great-hearted had yielded to his arms,
meaning the leaders by this figure.
The stork, renowned for its piety, in its nest high in the air
warms its unfledged chicks, its dear pledges,
and expects such gifts to be returned to it in turn
whenever, grown old, the mother will need this help.
Nor does the pious offspring deceive the hope, but carries on its shoulders
the weary bodies of the parents and supplies them food with its beak.
On tombs, on one side of a marble column stands
a jug; on the other a hand-basin can be seen.
This form reminds us that justice was administered without filth
and that the deceased had clean hands.

29.motto: The good have nothing to fear from the rich.

reading: Joined to me by a common wall, Marius, and also
Subbardus, well-known names of our forum,
are building, well provided with money, and even go out of their way
to block, alas, our light on every side.
Wretched me, whom, like Phineus, two Harpies
drag about, to drive me out of my own home —
unless our integrity and our mind that seeks what is honourable
are Zetes against them, are Calais against them.
What cause moves you, Saturnian bird [the eagle],
to sit high upon the tomb of great Aristomenes?
This I proclaim: as much as I excel in strength among birds,
so much does Aristomenes among the demigods.
Let timid doves sit on the tombs of the timid;
we eagles give kindly signs to the fearless.
Sad fortune must be borne by man by enduring it,
and too happy fortune has often had to be feared.
“Bear and forbear,” Epictetus used to say: one must
endure much and keep one's hands from what is forbidden.
So the bull, tied by the right knee, bears the command
of its leader; so it holds itself back from the pregnant [cows].

32.motto: On one who does not know how to flatter.

reading: Do you wish to know why the Thessalian land so often changes
masters and seems to seek to have various rulers?
It does not know how to flatter or to press caresses on anyone,
a custom which every royal court of a prince has;
but like a well-bred horse it throws from its back any
groom who does not know how to manage it.
Yet the master is not permitted to rage; the only vengeance
is to order the wild one to bear a harsher bit.

33.motto: One must hold out against pressure.

reading: The palm strives against the weight and rises into an arch:
the more it is pressed, the higher it lifts the load.
And it bears fragrant fruits, sweet dainties,
which are given the first honour among the courses.
Go, boy, and climbing along the branches gather them: whoever is
constant of mind will win worthy rewards.

34.motto: I carry all my things with me.

reading: The poor Hun, most wretched dweller by the Scythian sea,
his limbs livid, burnt by perpetual frost,
who knows neither the riches of Ceres nor the gifts of Lyaeus,
and yet always has costly coverings:
for skins of mice wrap him tightly on every side.
Only his eyes are open; all the rest he keeps covered.
So he does not fear the thief, so he scorns winds and rains,
safe among men, safe among the gods.
Crows have an amazing concord of life among themselves,
and an inviolate mutual faith remains among them.
Hence sceptres bear these birds: because all
leaders stand and fall by the consent of the people.
If you remove it from their midst, headlong discord
flies in and drags royal doom along with it.
When Rome was preparing leaders for civil war
and the land of Mars was falling by its own strength,
it was the custom, when troops came together on the same side,
to give one another joined right hands as gifts.
This is the image of a covenant: Concord has this sign,
so that those whom love joins, the hand may also join.
Among three brothers there was concord,
so great a mutual devotion and a single love,
that, unconquered by human strength, they held wide
kingdoms and were called by one name, Geryon.

38.motto: One can do nothing, two very much.

reading: The son of Laertes, and together with him the son of Tydeus,
the skilled hand of Zenalis has portrayed in this wax.
This one excels in strength, that one is powerful in sharpness of mind,
and yet each needs the help of the other.
When the two come joined together, victory is certain;
a man alone is failed either by mind or by right hand.

39.motto: The most firmly rooted cannot be torn up.

reading: Though father Ocean should stir up all his waves,
and you, barbarian Turk, should drink the whole Danube,
yet you will not break through the shattered frontier, while Caesar
Charles gives the peoples the standards of war.
So the sacred oaks stand on firm roots,
though the winds shake their dry leaves.
Your commonwealth is tossed by countless storms,
and only hope of future safety is at hand:
just like a ship in the midst of the sea, which the winds
sweep along, and which is already breaking up in the salt waters.
But if the shining stars, the brothers of Helen, appear,
good hope restores lost courage.
What goddess is this, looking up at the stars with so joyful a face?
By whose brushes was this image rendered?
The hands of Elpidius made it. I am she who is called
Good Hope, who offers the wretched ready help.
Why is your cloak green? Because under my guidance all things bloom.
Why do you carry in your hands the broken arrows of death?
Because the living should hope; for the buried I cut hope off.
Why do you sit idly on the lid of a little jar?
I alone stayed at home when evils flew off in all directions,
as the revered muse of the old man of Ascra [Hesiod] taught.
What bird is that beside you? The crow, most faithful of omen-birds:
when it cannot say “it is well”, it says “it will be”.
Who are your companions? Good Outcome and headlong Cupid.
Who go before? They are called the empty dreams of the waking.
Who stands joined to you? The Rhamnusian [Nemesis], avenger of crimes,
that is, so that you may hope for nothing but what is permitted.
At the new year a client offered me the snout of a bristly pig,
and said: “Take this gift for your belly.”
It always moves forward and never looks back
when, greedy, it roots up the grass with its bent snout.
Men have the same concern: that hope should not slip and fall
back, and that what is further should be better.

43.motto: The unlawful is not to be hoped for.

reading: Hope and Nemesis are present together at our altars,
that is, so that you may hope for nothing but what is permitted.
If the wife of the porphyrion commits adultery in her master's house,
he loses heart and dies of grief.
The cause is hidden in the secrets of nature. Let this bird
be a sure sign of pure chastity.

45.motto: On a victory won by guile.

reading: I, Virtue, bathe the tomb of Ajax with tears,
alas, wretched, having torn my whitening hair.
This, of course, was still left: that by a Greek judge
I should be defeated, and that guile should prevail over the better cause.
The little lizard, the stellio, its body starred with dark
spots, which haunts hiding places and hollow tombs,
when depicted carries the symbols of envy and wicked guile;
alas, all too well known to jealous wives.
For anyone's face is covered with ugly freckles
who drinks wine in which a stellio has been steeped.
Hence the frequent revenge by wine [of a wife] deceived by a mistress:
the lover abandons her once the flower of her beauty is lost.
A fattened decoy duck, blue in its plumage,
and accustomed to go back and forth to its masters,
seeing flocks of its own kind flying through the air,
quacks, and joins their flock,
until it leads the unwary under the spread nets.
The captives make an uproar, but she herself, knowing, is silent.
The treacherous bird pollutes itself with kindred blood,
obliging to others, deadly to its own.
They say that on the tomb of Archilochus there are wasps carved in marble,
sure seals of an evil tongue.
A band of robbers and thieves, Scaeva, goes through the city
as your retinue, and a cohort girt with dreadful swords.
And so, spendthrift, you consider yourself generous of spirit,
because your pot attracts many villains.
Behold a new Actaeon, who, after he had put on horns,
gave himself as prey to his own dogs.
Always gaping, always the thin air on which it feeds
the chameleon breathes in and out,
and changes its appearance and takes on various colours,
except red or white.
So too the flatterer feeds on the breeze of popular favour,
and, gaping, devours everything,
and imitates only the black ways of the prince,
knowing nothing of the white and modest.

51.motto: To one who has once squandered his own, others' goods should not be entrusted.

reading: Why do you build your nest in the bosom of the Colchian woman? Alas,
ignorant bird, why do you entrust your chicks so badly?
Medea, a dreadful mother, most cruel, destroyed
her own children, and do you hope that she will spare yours?
Headlong he is swept along, and in vain he pulls at the reins,
the driver carried by a horse with an unbridled mouth.
You would not easily trust one whom no reason governs
and who is rashly led by his own will.
The shield bears the painted face of a raging lion
and has a verse written on its upper rim:
“This is the terror of men”; its owner, the son of Atreus,
great-hearted Agamemnon, bore such devices.
You see Phaethon, driver of his father's chariot,
who dared to steer the fire-breathing horses of the Sun.
After he had scattered the greatest fires over the earth,
the wretch fell from the axle he had rashly mounted.
So too most kings, raised to the stars by the wheels of Fortune,
whom youthful ambition drives,
after great ruin of the human race and their own,
at last pay the penalty for all their crimes.

55.motto: On those who dare anything beyond their strength.

reading: While he sleeps, while he refreshes his body with sweet sleep
under a spruce, and holds his club and his other weapons,
the band of Pygmies thinks it can put Alcides
to death, poorly aware of its own strength.
Awakened, he crushes the enemy like fleas,
and drives them along wrapped in the skin of the savage lion.
You wash an Ethiopian: why in vain? Ah, stop. The darkness
of black night no one can light up.
Why do many call country folk, the rustic kind,
cuckoos, and what cause has been given for it?
In early spring the cuckoo (coccyx) sings; whoever by that time
has not finished [the work on] his vines is rightly marked as idle.
It lays its eggs in others' nests, like the man
whose marriage bed his wife betrays by adultery.
That he took his name from the bird, the daughter of Minyas (Meneis) [the bat]:
so the authors report of Chaerephon the Socratic.
The man had a swarthy face and a squeaky little voice: with such
a mark could this man be branded.
She who flies only at evening, who is weak of sight,
who, though she bears wings, has all else of a mouse,
is applied to different things. First she signifies
men of bad name, who lurk and fear judgment.
Next, philosophers too, who, while they seek heavenly things,
grow dim of eye and see only what is false.
Lastly, the crafty too, who, secretly following both [sides],
win trust with neither side.
The ancients called the lion's tail the alcaea:
spurred by it, he conceives heavy wrath.
When the yellow bile rises, and pain grows raw
with black gall, it rouses untamed fury.

61.motto: On one who prepares harm for himself.

reading: I, the goat, not of my own will, now suckle a wolf at my udder,
because the ill-provident care of the shepherd orders it.
As soon as he has grown, after my udder he will feed on me.
Wickedness is not softened by any kindness.
You wonder that in our song you are called Otus,
since you have from your forefathers the ancient name Otho.
It is an eared bird, and has feathers like an owl's,
and the skilful fowler takes the bird while it dances.
Hence we call fools, and those easy to catch, “oti”;
you too, have this name that suits you.

63.motto: Forgetfulness is the mother of poverty.

reading: When the hungry lynx (lupus cervarius) is chewing its food
and from hunger devours a captured fawn,
if by chance it looks elsewhere or turns its eyes,
forgetting the present food it holds in its claw,
it seeks uncertain prey (so great is its forgetfulness).
He who foolishly neglected his own seeks what belongs to others.
Behold a statue of a statue, marble carved out of marble:
insolent Niobe, who dared to compare herself with the gods.
Pride is a woman's vice, and it betrays a hardness
of face and feeling such as is in stone.
A woman down to the groin, girt below with the barking
whelps of monsters: such was two-formed Scylla.
Avarice, boldness, rapine are held to be the monsters.
But Scylla is the one in whose face there is no shame.
Because your beauty [pleased] you too much, Narcissus [?],
it has been turned into a flower and the plant of well-known numbness (νάρκη).
Self-love is the withering and ruin of talent: it
ruins and has ruined many learned men,
who, casting aside the method of the ancients, seek new doctrines
and hand down nothing but their own fantasies.
Why, chattering Procne, do you break my morning sleep,
and sing, Daulian, with your noisy mouth?
Tereus deserved to be a hoopoe, he who preferred to prune with the sword
rather than to root out the immoderate tongue.
A squalid woman chewing the flesh of vipers,
whose eyes ache and who eats her own heart,
whom leanness and pallor possess, and who carries thorny
darts in her hand: thus is Envy depicted.
Goat-footed Faunus, his temples wreathed with rocket (eruca),
displays the sure symbols of immoderate Venus.
Rocket is lustful, the he-goat is the betrayer of lust,
and satyrs are always wont to love nymphs.
On airy cliffs and on the edge of a high rock
the bitter fig tree bears ungentle fruits,
which ravens eat, which the shameless crow devours,
and which have nothing of use for man.
So parasites and harlots enjoy the riches of fools,
and they help the just with no benefit.

71.subheading: Διαλογιστικῶς (“In the form of a dialogue”).

reading: What tomb is this? Whose urn? It is that of Lais of Ephyra.
Ah, did not
the Fate blush to destroy such beauty?
There was no beauty then: age had already plucked it,
and the old woman had already prudently dedicated her mirror to Venus.
What does the carved ram mean, which a lioness
holds, seized with her claws by its hind part?
That she too held her captured lovers in the same way:
the ram is the husband of the flock; the lover is held by the haunch (clunis).

greek.translation: In the form of a dialogue.

reading: A fisherman, clothed in the covering of a shaggy goat,
having added two horns to his head,
standing at the very edge of the shore, deceives the amorous sargus,
which desire for the snub-nosed flock drives into the snares.
The goat represents the harlot; the sargus becomes like the lover,
who, wretched, perishes, caught by obscene love.
So great is said to have been the power of Circe, child of the Sun,
that she turned many men into strange monsters.
Witness Picus, tamer of horses, then two-formed Scylla,
and the [companions] of the Ithacan, swine after they had drunk the wine.
Circe, with a famous name, signifies the harlot,
and [shows] that whoever loves loses the reason of his mind.
Adonis, pierced in the groin by the savage tusk, Cypris
laid lifeless in the leaves of lettuce.
Hence lettuce resists the genital field as much
as lustful rocket can barely stimulate it.
So that dire love may not conquer you, and that no woman
may tear your mind apart with magic arts,
let the Bacchic bird, the wagtail, be ready for you,
which you are to place four-rayed in the round of a wheel,
so that it may form a cross with beak, tail and both wings:
such an amulet will be [proof] against every spell.
By this sign of Venus, it is said, Pagasaean Jason
could not be harmed by the wiles of the Phasis [of Colchis].
The white mouse is believed to signify luxury
and softness, but the reason is not quite clear to me.
Is it because its nature is lustful and its desire great?
Or because it adorns Roman wives with its fur?
Many call the Sarmatian mouse the sable (zibellus),
and the Arabian musk is famous for its sweet ointment.
The Essene sits idle in a bushel measure (modius), a watcher of the stars,
and beneath it hides a torch lit with fire.
Sloth under the guise of righteousness, veiled by a cowl,
benefits neither itself nor others.
Let whoever is idle go away. For to sit down on the choenix [a grain measure]
the holy teachings of the old man of Samos [Pythagoras] forbid us.
Rise, then, and accustom your hands to hard labour,
so that tomorrow's hour may give you your measured food.

79.motto: On those who easily fall away from virtue.

reading: As the little remora, scorning the force of the wind
and of the oars (remorum), alone can stop a ship,
so some men, borne by talent and virtue towards the stars,
are held back in mid-course by a trifling cause:
such as an anxious lawsuit, or the passion for harlots
which draws young men away from excellent studies.
An ancient tale held that the starry heron portrays an idle slave,
both his pursuits and his manners.
It invented that the servant Asterias took the shape of the bird:
let the credit for this rest with the historians.
It is like a degenerate falcon which [?] in the air,
called “ardelio” [a busy idler] by the ancient poets.
